Q: How to find out which processes are using swap space in Linux? A:

Use smem

smem -s swap -r

Here is a link which tells you both how to install it (spoiler : usually apt install smem or equivalent) and how to use it: http://www.cyberciti.biz/faq/linux-which-process-is-using-swap/

Q: Now that `finalize()` is deprecated in Java, what should be used instead, especially for a global singleton? A:

Cleaner

Java 9 introduced the Cleaner and Cleanable utility classes from the java.lang.ref package. These take care of wiring up phantom references to a queue and a cleaning thread draining that queue.

While this lets you separate out the witness that will perform a post-mortem cleanup after the owning object has died, all the caveats about GC-triggered resource management still apply, i.e. it is still preferable to rely on AutoCloseable and try-with-resources blocks to manage the lifecycle of resources, not on the garbage collector.

Q: Getting rows when it has multiple rows or only one row in another table based on a column value A:

You can use EXISTS to check for the appropriate relationships between the two tables.

get all family_ids when it has only one type = 'multiple'

SELECT family_id,
       COUNT(*)
FROM   familys f
WHERE  EXISTS (
         SELECT 1
         FROM   types it
         WHERE  f.family_id = it.family_fk
         GROUP BY it.family_fk
         HAVING COUNT(CASE it.type WHEN 'multiple' THEN 1 END) = 1
         AND    COUNT(CASE it.type WHEN 'multiple' THEN NULL ELSE 1 END) = 0
       )
GROUP BY family_id

get all family_ids when it has more than one type including a type= 'multiple'

SELECT family_id,
       COUNT(*)
FROM   familys f
WHERE  EXISTS (
         SELECT 1
         FROM   types it
         WHERE  f.family_id = it.family_fk
         AND    it.type = 'multiple'
       )
GROUP BY family_id;

Q: How to convert a pandas dataframe to numeric future proof? A:

This solution adapted from here is good enough if you're working with floats :

df = df.apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").fillna(df)

But as noted by @mozway in comments, columns with errors are coerced into float64, since "coerce" introduces NaNs.
